facts.statement: The genus Parasaurolophus was first described by William Parks in 1922.
facts.quote: authority: Parks, 1922

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Campanian stage, with possible records from the Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Cretaceous (Campanian), Possible record during the Maastrichtian

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus lived approximately 76.5 to 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: about 76.5–73 million years ago

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus inhabited western North America and possibly Asia.
facts.quote: lived in what is now western North America and possibly Asia

facts.statement: The type specimen was a skull and partial skeleton discovered in Alberta.
facts.quote: The genus was first described in 1922 by William Parks from a skull and partial skeleton found in Alberta.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus was a large herbivore reaching over 9 meters in length and weighing over 5 metric tons.
facts.quote: It was a large herbivore that could reach over 9 m long and weigh over 5 MT

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus could move both bipedally and quadrupedally.
facts.quote: were able to move as a biped and a quadruped

facts.statement: The genus is characterized by a large, elaborate cranial crest forming a long curved tube.
facts.quote: This genus is known for its large, elaborate cranial crest, which forms a long curved tube projecting upwards and back from the skull in its largest form.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was found in 1920 by a University of Toronto field party near Sand Creek in Alberta.
facts.quote: found by a field party from the University of Toronto in 1920 near Sand Creek along the Red Deer River in Alberta.

facts.statement: The rocks containing the type specimen belong to the Campanian-age Dinosaur Park Formation.
facts.quote: These rocks are now known as the Campanian age Late Cretaceous period Dinosaur Park Formation.

facts.statement: The species name P. walkeri honors Sir Byron Edmund Walker.
facts.quote: William Parks named the specimen P. walkeri in honor of Sir Byron Edmund Walker

facts.statement: A partial skull was recovered in 1921 from the Kirtland Formation in New Mexico.
facts.quote: In 1921, Charles H. Sternberg recovered a partial skull (PMU.R1250) from what is now known as the slightly younger Kirtland Formation in San Juan County, New Mexico.

facts.statement: Carl Wiman described the New Mexico specimen as the species P. tubicen in 1931.
facts.quote: where Carl Wiman described it as a second species, P. tubicen, in 1931.

facts.statement: A nearly complete P. tubicen skull was discovered in New Mexico in 1995.
facts.quote: A second, nearly complete P. tubicen skull (NMMNH P-25100) was found in New Mexico in 1995.

facts.statement: John Ostrom described a New Mexico specimen as P. cyrtocristatus in 1961.
facts.quote: John Ostrom described another good specimen (FMNH P27393) from New Mexico as P. cyrtocristatus in 1961.

facts.statement: Three species are universally recognized: P. walkeri, P. tubicen, and P. cyrtocristatus.
facts.quote: Three species are universally recognized: P. walkeri (the type species), P. tubicen, and the short-crested P. cyrtocristatus.

facts.statement: P. tubicen is the largest of the Parasaurolophus species.
facts.quote: The next named species is P. tubicen, which is the largest of the Parasaurolophus species.

facts.statement: P. cyrtocristatus is the smallest species and possesses the most curved crest.
facts.quote: Of the Parasaurolophus species, P. cyrtocristatus is the smallest and has the most curved crest.

facts.statement: It has been speculated that P. cyrtocristatus represents a female of P. walkeri or P. tubicen.
facts.quote: it has often been speculated that it was a female of P. walkeri or P. tubicen

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding whether P. cyrtocristatus is a female of other species, with some studies supporting this and others refuting it based on age, distribution, and crest structure differences.
facts.quote: Even though many scientists have supported the possible fact of P. cyrtocristatus being a female, many other studies have found that it is not because of the differences in age, distribution, and the large differences in the crest and its internal structure.

facts.statement: A 2014 study suggested that Charonosaurus jiayensis might be nested within Parasaurolophus as P. jiayensis.
facts.quote: A study published in PLoS ONE in 2014 found that one more species could be referred to Parasaurolophus.

facts.statement: The type specimen of P. walkeri is estimated to be 9.45 meters long.
facts.quote: The length of the type specimen of P. walkeri is estimated at 9.45 m

facts.statement: Allometric estimates suggest a 9-meter individual weighed more than 5 metric tons.
facts.quote: allometry-based body mass estimates indicate that a 9 m long individual would have weighed more than 5 MT

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the average adult P. walkeri to be 7.5 meters long and weigh 2.6 metric tons.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul estimated that an average adult individual of the type species would measure 7.5 m long and weigh 2.6 MT.

facts.statement: The skull of the P. walkeri type specimen, including the crest, is about 1.6 meters long.
facts.quote: The skull of the P. walkeri type specimen is about 1.6 m long, including the crest.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus likely preferred to forage quadrupedally but ran bipedally.
facts.quote: It probably preferred to forage for food on four legs, but ran on two.

facts.statement: Skin impressions of P. walkeri show uniform tubercle-like scales without larger structures.
facts.quote: Skin impressions are known for P. walkeri, showing uniform tubercle-like scales, but no larger structures.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus is characterized by a large cranial crest located at the rear of the head, composed of the premaxilla and nasal bones.
facts.quote: The most noticeable feature was the cranial crest that protruded from the rear of the head and was made up of the premaxilla and nasal bones.

facts.statement: The crest of Parasaurolophus was hollow and contained tubes connecting the nostrils to the base of the skull.
facts.quote: The crest was hollow, with distinct tubes leading from each nostril to the end of the crest before reversing direction and heading back down the crest and into the skull.

facts.statement: P. walkeri and P. tubicen possessed long, slightly curved crests, whereas P. cyrtocristatus had a short, circular crest.
facts.quote: While P. walkeri and P. tubicen had long crests with slight curvature, P. cyrtocristatus had a short crest with a more circular profile.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus is classified as a member of the lambeosaurine subfamily within the hadrosaurids, distinct from the hadrosaurine Saurolophus.
facts.quote: However, it was soon reassessed as a member of the lambeosaurine subfamily of hadrosaurids—Saurolophus is a hadrosaurine.

facts.statement: Charonosaurus from the Amur region of northeastern China is considered the closest known relative of Parasaurolophus.
facts.quote: Its closest known relative appears to be Charonosaurus, a lambeosaurine with a similar skull (but no complete crest yet) from the Amur region of northeastern China.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus and Charonosaurus may together form the clade Parasaurolophini.
facts.quote: The two may form the clade called Parasaurolophini.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus was a large herbivore capable of both bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion that used a grinding motion to process plants.
facts.quote: As a hadrosaurid, Parasaurolophus was a large bipedal and quadrupedal herbivore, eating plants with a sophisticated skull that permitted a grinding motion analogous to chewing.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus possessed dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth that were continuously replaced, with only a few in use at any given time.
facts.quote: Its teeth were continually being replaced and were packed into dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth, but only a relative handful of which were in use at any time.

facts.statement: Parasaurolophus could feed on vegetation ranging from the ground up to a height of approximately 4 meters.
facts.quote: Vegetation could have been taken from the ground up to a height of around 4 m.

facts.statement: A juvenile Parasaurolophus specimen numbered RAM 14000 and nicknamed 'Joe' was described in 2013.
facts.quote: Parasaurolophus is known from many adult specimens, and a juvenile described in 2013, numbered RAM 14000 and nicknamed Joe, after a volunteer at the Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology (RAM).

facts.statement: Juvenile Parasaurolophus possessed a low, hemispherical crest, unlike the long and tubular crests of adults.
facts.quote: The crest of the juvenile is not long and tubular like the adults, but low and hemispherical.

facts.statement: Many hypotheses regarding the function of the Parasaurolophus cranial crest have been proposed, though most have been discredited.
facts.quote: Many hypotheses have been advanced as to what functions the cranial crest of Parasaurolophus performed, but most have been discredited.

facts.statement: Current theories suggest the Parasaurolophus crest served functions such as visual display, sound amplification, and thermoregulation.
facts.quote: It is now believed that it may have had several functions: visual display for identifying species and sex, sound amplification for communication, and thermoregulation.

facts.statement: It remains unclear which function of the Parasaurolophus crest was most significant during different stages of its evolution.
facts.quote: It is not clear which was most significant at what times in the evolution of the crest and its internal nasal passages.

facts.statement: James Hopson hypothesized that P. cyrtocristatus represented the female form of P. tubicen due to its smaller crest.
facts.quote: James Hopson, one of the first researchers to describe lambeosaurine crests in terms of such distinctions, suggested that P. cyrtocristatus, with its small crest, was the female form of P. tubicen.

facts.statement: Thomas Williamson suggested P. cyrtocristatus was the juvenile form of P. tubicen, but this hypothesis was not widely accepted.
facts.quote: Thomas Williamson suggested it was the juvenile form. Neither hypothesis became widely accepted.

facts.statement: The relationship between P. cyrtocristatus and P. tubicen remains debated due to the scarcity of known specimens.
facts.quote: As only six good skulls, one juvenile braincase, and one recently discovered juvenile skull are known, additional material will help clear up these potential relationships.

facts.statement: Early hypotheses suggested Parasaurolophus had adaptations for an aquatic lifestyle, a view common until the 1960s.
facts.quote: Many early suggestions focused on adaptations for an aquatic lifestyle, following the hypothesis that hadrosaurids were amphibious, a common line of thought until the 1960s.

facts.statement: Researchers proposed various aquatic functions for the crest, including acting as a snorkel, attachment for a proboscis, air trap, or air reservoir for underwater stays.
facts.quote: Alfred Sherwood Romer proposed it served as a snorkel, Martin Wilfarth that it was an attachment for a mobile proboscis used as a breathing tube or for food gathering, Charles M. Sternberg that it served as an airtrap to keep water out of the lungs, and Ned Colbert that it served as an air reservoir for prolonged stays underwater.

facts.statement: In 1922, William Parks suggested the crest was attached to vertebrae above the shoulders to help move and support the head.
facts.quote: William Parks, in 1922, suggested that the crest was joined to the vertebrae above the shoulders by ligaments or muscles, and helped with moving and supporting the head.

facts.statement: Othenio Abel proposed the crest was used as a weapon in combat, while Andrew Milner suggested it acted as a foliage deflector similar to a cassowary's casque.
facts.quote: Othenio Abel proposed it was used as a weapon in combat among members of the same species, and Andrew Milner suggested that it could be used as a foliage deflector, like the helmet crest (called a 'casque') of the cassowary.

facts.statement: Halszka Osmólska and John Ostrom hypothesized the crest housed salt glands or expanded olfactory tissue to improve smell.
facts.quote: Halszka Osmólska suggested that it housed salt glands, and John Ostrom suggested that it housed expanded areas for olfactory tissue and much improved sense of smell of the lambeosaurines, which had no obvious defensive capabilities.

facts.statement: Most early hypotheses regarding the crest's function have been discredited, such as the snorkel theory, because there is no hole at the crest's end.
facts.quote: Most of these hypotheses have been discredited or rejected. For example, there is no hole at the end of the crest for a snorkeling function.

facts.statement: Studies show olfactory nerves and sensory tissue in lambeosaurines were largely outside the crest, indicating the crest's expansion was not primarily for smell.
facts.quote: Additionally, work on the nasal cavity of lambeosaurines shows that olfactory nerves and corresponding sensory tissue were largely outside the portion of the nasal passages in the crest, so the expansion of the crest had little to do with the sense of smell.

facts.statement: The crest's large surface area and vascularization suggest it may have functioned in temperature regulation.
facts.quote: The large surface area and vascularization of the crest also suggests a thermoregulatory function.

facts.statement: Wheeler (1978) was the first to propose the crest related to temperature regulation, suggesting a nerve connection allowed the brain to be cooled by the crest.
facts.quote: The first to propose the cranial crests of lambeosaurines related to temperature regulation was Wheeler (1978). He proposed that there was a nerve connection between the crest and the brain, so that the latter could be cooled by the former.

facts.statement: In 2006, Evans argued that temperature regulation could be a factor driving the evolution of lambeosaurine crests.
facts.quote: In 2006 Evans published an argument about the functions of lambeosaurine crests, and supported why this could be a causing factor for the evolution of the crest.

facts.statement: Wiman (1931) originally suggested the crest functioned as a resonating chamber, noting its similarity to a swan's internal structures.
facts.quote: This function was originally suggested by Wiman in 1931 when he described P. tubicen. He noted that the crest's internal structures are similar to those of a swan and theorized that an animal could use its elongated nasal passages to create noise.

facts.statement: Weishampel (1981) suggested Parasaurolophus produced noises between 55 and 720 Hz, with ranges varying by species and potentially indicating sex.
facts.quote: Weishampel in 1981 suggested that Parasaurolophus made noises ranging between the frequencies 55 and 720 Hz, although there was some difference in the range of individual species because of the crest size, shape, and nasal passage length, most obvious in P. cyrtocristatus (interpreted as a possible female).

facts.statement: Computer modeling of a P. tubicen specimen allowed reconstruction of the sounds its crest could produce.
facts.quote: Computer modeling of a well-preserved specimen of P. tubicen, with more complex air passages than those of P. walkeri, has allowed the reconstruction of the possible sound its crest produced.

facts.statement: Modeling indicates the main resonant frequency of the crest is around 30 Hz, with variations caused by sinus anatomy.
facts.quote: The main path resonates at around 30 Hz, but the complicated sinus anatomy causes peaks and valleys in the sound.

facts.statement: Another theory suggests the crest was used for intra-species recognition, serving as a warning signal or for other non-sexual purposes.
facts.quote: The other main behavioral theory is that the crest was used for intra-species recognition. This means that the crest could have been used for species recognition, as a warning signal, and for other, non-sexual uses.

facts.statement: The crest likely served as a visual signal to distinguish Parasaurolophus from its contemporaries.
facts.quote: As a large object, the crest has clear value as a visual signal and sets this animal apart from its contemporaries.

facts.statement: The crest likely allowed for both species identification and sexual identification based on shape and size.
facts.quote: As is suggested by other lambeosaurine skulls, the crest of Parasaurolophus likely permitted both species identification (such as separating it from Corythosaurus or Lambeosaurus) and sexual identification by shape and size.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown (1912) hypothesized fine striations near the crest indicated a skin frill similar to that of a basilisk lizard.
facts.quote: Barnum Brown (1912) noted the presence of fine striations near the back of the crest that he hypothesized could be associated with the presence of a frill of skin, comparable to the one found in the modern basilisk lizard.

facts.statement: A specimen of P. walkeri shows a V-shaped gap or notch in the vertebrae at the base of the neck, possibly indicating a pathology.
facts.quote: P. walkeri is known from one specimen which might contain a pathology. The skeleton shows a v-shaped gap or notch in the vertebrae at the base of the neck.

facts.statement: Analysis by Bertozzo et al. (December 2020) suggests pathologies in the holotype of P. walkeri were likely caused by being hit by a falling tree during a storm.
facts.quote: Analysis of the pathology undertaken by Bertozzo et al., published in December 2020, suggests the pathology to the shoulder and thoracic ribs in the holotype of P. walkeri was plausibly the result of the dinosaur being hit by a falling tree, perhaps during a severe storm.
